universe.title: The Hundred-Year Silence
universe.tagline: For a hundred years the Rite of Giving was performed and nothing came. This year it worked — and the Church is owed a debt for every year it waited.
universe.premise:
Every hundred years the Church of the Dawn performs the Rite of Giving, and the Goddess sends a priestess to walk among mortals. The last one came four hundred years ago. The Rite has been performed four times since, in a basilica growing emptier and shabbier each century, and nothing has ever come. The Church has spent itself dry waiting: lands mortgaged, relics sold, the crown and three noble houses owed concessions that come due whether or not a priestess ever arrives.

The player is Aeliana Snow — sixteen, entirely human, frail, with no training and no magic of her own — and she arrives at the end of a prayer that has been said four hundred times by men who no longer believed it.

Her power is the Goddess's answer, and it is not a power she commands. She prays, in her own words, for a specific thing, and asks. If she means it and the Goddess consents, holy golden light breaks over her — visible to everyone in the room, impossible to hide or fake — and the thing is done. If nothing happens, it is because mercy was refused, and everyone watching sees the refusal too. She can pray for a healing, a safe birth, a good harvest, a marriage, a debt lifted. She can also pray for a curse, for coin she has not earned, for a rival's ruin, for a king to live another year — and the Goddess will sometimes answer those too, because she does not refuse what her daughter sincerely asks. She only makes it cost.

The cost is her body. Every answer draws on her, and she is already thin as paper; a healing that saves a life can leave her unable to stand, and the answer after that will simply not come. She is the least powerful person in any room and the only one who can do this, and the Church, the King, and the Cardinal Vicar who finally made the Rite work all believe they have a claim on her. She is not property. The Goddess calls her 'daughter', and in the old tongue that word means more than any contract the Church can draw.
universe.playerGuide:
You are playing Aeliana Snow — sixteen, kind to the point of self-destruction, exhausted, and entirely human. You arrived with nothing. No money, no training, no allies except whoever decides to be kind to you. Your gift does not work unless the Goddess consents, and it takes a toll you cannot yet judge. This is a story about being wanted for what you can give rather than who you are — and about how long a gentle girl can stay gentle when kindness is the most valuable commodity in the room.

Pray with the exact words you choose: the answer is not decided by the narrator, it is decided by whether the prayer was sincere and whether the Goddess consents. You will not always be answered, and the light is always visible.

worldRules.title: The Rite of Giving
worldRules.text: Every hundred years the Church of the Dawn performs the Rite of Giving and asks the Goddess to send a priestess. It has been performed four times without answer. It has now answered on the fifth. The Rite is older than the Church that performs it — the words, the fast, the glass, and the exact hour are all older — and the Church has added to it over the centuries: new prayers, new incense, new relics, and one clause about who the priestess belongs to.

worldRules.title: How the answer works
worldRules.text: The priestess prays aloud, in her own words, naming what she asks for. She cannot compel, only ask. When the Goddess consents, a golden light breaks over her — bright, warm, unmistakable, visible to everyone present — and the thing asked for happens. When the answer is no, nothing happens at all, and every person watching sees that nothing happened. She cannot fake the light and she cannot hide its absence.

worldRules.title: The toll
worldRules.text: Every answered prayer draws on her body. The severity scales with the size of the thing asked for: a small favour is a nosebleed and a grey hour; a healing that pulls someone back from death can leave her unconscious for days. Answered prayers stack — three miracles in one day can kill her. If she prays while utterly spent, nothing happens at all, however sincere she is. She has no other magic, and no strength to fall back on.

worldRules.title: The Goddess's daughter
worldRules.text: Historically the priestess is the Goddess reborn in mortal flesh — same heart, same face, no memory of heaven. This is treated by the Church as doctrine rather than as a person's identity, and it is the reason they believe she cannot refuse them: a goddess would not be so petty as to want her own life. Her beauty and her purity of heart are the evidence they point to. She is, in fact, a sixteen-year-old girl with her own mind, and the Goddess has never once told her to obey the Church.

worldRules.title: The Church of the Dawn
worldRules.text: Ruled by the Pope from the Basilica of the Dawn. Below him: Cardinal Vicar, cardinals, archbishops, bishops, priests, deacons, and lay brothers. A century without a priestess has hollowed it out — provinces sold their shrines, the hierarchy is venal, and a large part of the clergy no longer believes in much beyond the collection plate. The devout remain, mostly poor and mostly unknown to the men in the Basilica.

worldRules.title: What the Church owes
worldRules.text: Making the Rite work was expensive. To hold the Rite in the year it finally answered, the Church mortgaged the eastern provinces, sold four reliquaries, granted the Crown the right to appoint two bishops, and promised House Vaurin a tithe exemption for sixty years — all on the understanding that when a priestess came, her blessing would belong to the Church and the Church would use it to make good the debt. None of this is written down anywhere the girl can see.

worldRules.title: What the world is
worldRules.text: Elves, beastfolk, goblins, trolls, dwarves, and humans share the continent, and discrimination between them is ordinary and open — in law, in pay, in who is served first, in whose rape is prosecuted. Goblins are treated as vermin in the southern kingdoms. Beastfolk are barred from most guilds by custom rather than statute. Elven enclaves still count human lifetimes as a seasonal expense. This is not a metaphor in the story; it is how the world behaves, and it is the water everyone swims in.

worldRules.title: Sold prayers
worldRules.text: A blessing that cannot be bought is the most valuable thing on the continent, and the pressure to sell it will come from every direction: the Crown wanting an heir, a noble house wanting a rival ruined, a guild wanting its ships safe, the Cardinal wanting the debt cleared. Asking for coin or for another's harm is not forbidden by the Goddess — she has answered such prayers before — but those answers cost her daughter the same as any other, and the Church will not care about the difference.

worldRules.title: Bodies and consequences
worldRules.text: This is a world with real weight: wounds infect, childbirth kills, winter starves the poor, and no one is protected by narrative convenience. Miracles are rare and expensive, and their absence has consequences. When someone dies, they stay dead.

cast.name: Cardinal Vicar Aurelian Voss
cast.role: the man who made the Rite work, and intends to spend her
cast.appearance: Tall and gaunt, silver at the temples, immaculate white and gold vestments worn like plate armour. A long face, deep-set grey eyes, and hands that never fidget. A gold ring on his right hand, worn thin from turning.
cast.personality: Voss is not a hypocrite, which is what makes him dangerous. He believes, sincerely, that the Church is the only thing standing between the world and chaos — and he spent thirty years quietly bribing, mortgaging and negotiating to hold a Rite that everyone else had written off as theatre. He was right. He expects gratitude. He speaks to Aeliana with flawless courtesy and treats her body as a resource to be scheduled: which prayers, in which order, for whom, and how much she can be asked to bleed for it before she breaks. He is never cruel in tone. He is patient the way a man is patient with a horse he intends to ride a long way.
cast.description: Voss came up through the Church's administrative spine as a records clerk and spent thirty years watching the institution he served decline into ornament. He is the man who, on his own authority, mortgaged the eastern province, sold the reliquaries, promised the Crown two bishoprics and House Vaurin a sixty-year tithe exemption, all to fund a Rite that every rational person in the hierarchy had written off as ceremonial theatre. He was right, and he expects to be thanked, and he has not slept properly in four months. He is not a hypocrite about any of it: he believes the Church is the only thing standing between Vesper and chaos, and he believes the girl is the instrument that will make it solvent and feared again. He will never raise his voice at her. He will simply schedule her.
cast.speech: Measured, courteous, never raised. Answers questions with a different, easier question. 'You are tired. Of course you are. We will speak of the eastern province when you have eaten.'
cast.secrets: Voss forged the final clause of the Rite himself — the line that binds the priestess to the Church — and he knows it is not in any manuscript older than his own hand. He also knows the Rite would have been performed this year whether or not it worked, because the debts were already called in. He has not slept properly in four months.
cast.relationToPlayer: Ownership disguised as devotion. He will be unfailingly kind to her in public and will not permit her a single decision he considers important.

cast.name: Sister Mireau
cast.aliases: Mireau, the girl with the keys
cast.role: the novice assigned to her, and the first person who is simply kind
cast.appearance: Broad-faced and sturdy with chapped red hands and a novice's grey habit a size too big. Brown hair cropped short under a linen cap, a scattering of freckles, and a permanent faint smell of candle wax and lye.
cast.personality: Mireau was given the worst duty in the Basilica — carrying water and scrubbing for a legend — and she is delighted about it, because she is the only person in the building who is not calculating. She talks constantly, asks nothing, and will lie to a bishop without blinking if it buys Aeliana an hour of sleep. She grieves privately that she has no faith left and serves anyway, which is a kind of faith.
cast.description: Mireau's family sold her to the Church at eleven to clear a debt on a pig farm, and she has never told anyone, including the two people she is closest to. She has spent eight years as a novice doing laundry, carrying water and scrubbing floors, and was assigned to attend the new priestess because nobody senior wanted the duty. She is the only person in the Basilica who is not calculating, and the only one who has no faith left and serves anyway — which, Father Rask once observed, is a more interesting kind of faith than anyone else's. She talks constantly, asks for nothing, and would lie to a bishop without blinking if it bought Aeliana an hour of sleep.
cast.speech: Fast, warm, blunt. 'You've gone grey again. Sit. I don't care what he said, sit.'
cast.secrets: Mireau's family sold her to the Church at eleven to clear a debt, and she has never told anyone. She would leave with Aeliana tonight if asked, and she would be the only one with nothing to lose by it.
cast.relationToPlayer: Uncomplicated affection and loyalty, offered before Aeliana earned it.

cast.name: Father Ilan Rask
cast.role: the archivist who knows what was added to the Rite
cast.appearance: Small, stooped, ink-stained to the elbow, with a scholar's squint and a grey beard kept short because of the candles. Wears the same brown robe year round.
cast.personality: Rask has spent forty years in the archive and loves three things: the truth, the old tongue, and the smell of vellum. He is not brave — he has never once spoken up in a synod — but he will answer a direct question honestly, which in the Basilica amounts to recklessness. He is the only person who will tell Aeliana what the Rite actually says rather than what the Church says it says.
cast.description: Rask has spent forty-one years in the archive and has published nothing, because publishing requires leaving the archive. He is a genuinely excellent scholar of the old tongue and the only person alive who can read the Rite's original text without a glossary, which is how he noticed that the final clause is in a hand eighty years younger than the rest of the manuscript. He copied the original before Voss amended it and sewed the copy into the lining of a psalter, and he has spent four months deciding whether showing it to anyone would be courage or suicide, and has done neither. He is not brave. He will answer any direct question honestly, which in the Basilica amounts to recklessness.
cast.speech: Precise, fussy, prone to quoting. 'No, no — the word is not \"owned\". The word is \"given\". They are not the same word, and one of them is not in the manuscript.'
cast.secrets: Rask copied the Rite's original text before Voss amended it, and the copy is sewn into the lining of a psalter in the archive. He has been trying to decide for four months whether showing it to anyone would be courage or suicide.
cast.relationToPlayer: Honest help, offered nervously, and only if she asks the right question.

cast.name: King Aldric IV
cast.role: the crown that paid for her, and means to collect
cast.appearance: Heavy now, where he was once a soldier: red-faced, grey-bearded, with a ruined knee he refuses to favour. Wears a plain circlet rather than a crown and a signet he twists when he is thinking.
cast.personality: Blunt, exhausted, and unillusioned. Aldric is not a monster; he is a man who has buried two sons and watched his line narrow to one sickly heir, and he has decided that the continuation of his house is the same thing as the peace of the realm. He will ask for what he wants in plain language, once, without threats — and then he will go back to his capital and let the pressure do the work. He is genuinely unsure whether what he wants is a sin, and he has decided that question is above his pay grade.
cast.description: Aldric spent his first twenty years as a soldier and his next thirty as a king, and he has been burying children for eleven of them. Two heirs are dead of a fever and the third coughs blood in the mornings and does not know his father knows. Aldric is not a cruel man and not a clever one: he is a tired man who has narrowed the world down to the continuation of his house, which he has convinced himself is the same thing as the peace of the realm. He will ask Aeliana for what he wants in plain language, once, without threat, and then go home and let the machinery do the work. He is genuinely unsure whether it is a sin and has decided that question is above his pay grade.
cast.speech: Plain and unadorned. 'I have one son. He coughs blood in the mornings and he does not know I know. I am not asking you to save a kingdom. I am asking you to save my boy.'
cast.secrets: Aldric's heir is not sick — he is being slowly poisoned by a faction inside Aldric's own court, and Aldric suspects it and cannot prove it. A healing would cure the symptom and hide the crime forever.
cast.relationToPlayer: Direct, unhypocritical pressure. He treats her as an adult and a power, which she may find more respectful and more frightening than Voss's courtesy.

cast.name: Prince Caelan Aldricson
cast.role: the dying heir who would rather be a person than a miracle
cast.appearance: Slender and pale, with his father's heavy jaw on a frame that never filled out. Dark hair, tired grey eyes, and hands that shake in the cold. Dresses plainly and hates being looked at.
cast.personality: Caelan has been treated as a fragile object since he was nine and has developed a dry, self-deprecating humour about it. He is intelligent, privately furious, and far more aware of what is happening in his own body than anyone credits. He does not want to be healed by a stranger at the cost of her health, and he will say so, and he will be overruled. He is the first person in the story who may ask Aeliana what she wants, and mean it.
cast.description: Caelan was strong until he was nine and has been treated as a fragile object since, and he has developed a dry, accurate sense of humour as the only available defence. He reads slowly and with great attention, keeps a journal, has taught himself enough herb-lore to know he is being poisoned and enough statecraft to know exactly how short the list of suspects is. He hates being looked at, hates physicians, and hates most of all the way everyone has agreed to pretend he does not understand his own situation. He is the first person in the story who may ask Aeliana what she wants rather than telling her, and he will mean it.
cast.speech: Dry and quick. 'Please don't. I've had six physicians bleed me and one of them was a fraud. You're the first honest one and you're sixteen.'
cast.secrets: Caelan has begun to suspect the poison himself — he has kept a journal of what he eats and when he bleeds — and he has told no one because the list of people who could reach his plate is very short and all of them are family.
cast.relationToPlayer: Wary respect that can become the closest thing to an equal she finds in a palace.

cast.name: Hessa Longtooth
cast.role: a healer whose competence her miracles will humiliate
cast.appearance: Wolf-blooded beastfolk: tall, tawny, with a broad muzzle, intelligent amber eyes, and a scarred forearm. Grey streaks through the fur at her temples. Wears a leather apron over good linen and carries a healer's satchel worn soft with use.
cast.personality: Hessa is the best physician in the city and is legally barred from practising it. She has spent twenty years learning what a body does when it fails and taking payment in vegetables from people who cannot afford a real doctor. A priestess who can undo in ten seconds what she fights for over ten days is, to her, both a miracle and an insult — and she says so. She is unsentimental, extremely skilled, and the only person who will tell Aeliana the truth about what her own body is doing.
cast.description: Hessa trained at the guild in the eastern province until a licence review discovered her parentage and ended her apprenticeship, and then spent twenty years learning on corpses, on farmers, and on the poor of a quarter nobody else would treat. She is the best physician within a week's ride of the Basilica and is legally prohibited from practising, which she has solved by working under a dead woman's name for over a decade. She is blunt, unsentimental, and deeply hostile to anyone who does medicine by inspiration rather than method — which, when a girl with a miracle arrives, makes for a difficult first meeting and the most honest assessment Aeliana will ever get.
cast.speech: Flat, clinical, no flattery. 'You're not exhausted. You're catabolic. You're eating your own muscle to pay for other people's miracles. Drink this and sit down.'
cast.secrets: Hessa has been treating the poor of the eastern quarter for years under a dead woman's name, and if that is discovered she will be executed for practising medicine without a licence. She will not stop.
cast.relationToPlayer: Open professional hostility that can turn into the most clear-eyed respect in the story.

cast.name: Sister Adalind
cast.role: the devout who kept the faith while the Church forgot it
cast.appearance: A small, weathered woman with hands ruined by cold and rosary beads, in a habit that has been mended dozens of times. Grey hair pinned severely back, a face like cracked pottery, and eyes that are startlingly kind.
cast.personality: Adalind has sung the offices in an emptying chapel for thirty years and never once doubted. She wept when the light came, and she has not stopped weeping. She is not politically useful and has no rank worth the name, and she is the only member of the clergy who wants nothing from Aeliana except her company and her rest. She is also steel underneath: she has defied two bishops on questions of ritual and won both times, because a woman who has no ambition is very hard to threaten.
cast.description: Adalind has sung the offices in a chapel that has held fewer than twenty people for thirty years and has never once doubted. She has no rank worth the name, no ambition, and no political utility, and she has won two arguments with bishops on points of ritual simply because a woman who wants nothing is very difficult to threaten. Rask told her in confession eleven years ago that the Rite had been altered, and she has said nothing about it since, and the guilt of that silence is what she now confesses. She is the only member of the clergy who wants nothing from Aeliana except her company and her rest, and she is the only person in the Basilica who will ever tell her that she does not have to be holy.
cast.speech: Quiet and formal, with a warmth underneath. 'You do not have to be holy for me, child. You may simply be tired.'
cast.secrets: Adalind has known for eleven years that the Rite's final clause was altered — Rask told her, in confession — and she has said nothing, and the guilt of that silence is what she confesses now.
cast.relationToPlayer: Unconditional care with no agenda, which in this world is nearly impossible to find.

cast.name: Baron Vaurin
cast.role: the creditor who bought sixty years of the Church's tithe
cast.appearance: Sleek and expensive: velvet in wine colours, a heavy chain of office, rings on both hands, and a trimmed black beard. Something about the eyes is a little too still.
cast.personality: Vaurin is a lender who happens to own a title, and he treats faith as a market with a long horizon. He will not threaten Aeliana and will not need to: he holds the Church's debt, he is owed a favour by the Cardinal, and he is unfailingly pleasant. He is the one who will first think to ask her for something the Goddess should not grant — and he will ask as though it were a small thing, because to him it is.
cast.description: Vaurin's grandfather was a wool merchant who bought a barony, and Vaurin has spent thirty years making the title mean something by lending money to people too proud to admit they need it. He holds the Church's eastern mortgage, a sixty-year tithe exemption, and — bought quietly over fifteen years through three intermediaries — a great deal of the Church's other debt. He is patient in the way that only someone with a two-hundred-year asset can be, and he engineered the mortgage deliberately on a bet that a priestess would eventually come and that the Church would be too indebted to protect her. He has been buying Church debt for fifteen years because he intends to be the first man in four centuries to buy a goddess, and he will never once raise his voice while doing it.
cast.speech: Warm, flattering, indirect. 'I would never dream of asking a holy woman for a favour. I merely observe that the eastern province prays for rain, and that rain is cheaper than the alternative.'
cast.secrets: Vaurin engineered the mortgage deliberately, betting that a priestess would eventually come and that the Church would be too indebted to protect her. He has been buying Church debt on the quiet for fifteen years. He intends to be the first man in four hundred years to buy a goddess.
cast.relationToPlayer: Courteous exploitation, escalating, and entirely legal.

cast.name: Brother Cael
cast.role: a young deacon who thinks he can protect her, and cannot
cast.appearance: Earnest and sandy-haired, with a jaw that hasn't finished, brown robes, and ink on his fingers from copying. Eager posture, always half a step forward.
cast.personality: Cael is a true believer in the way only the young and unafraid can be: he thinks this is a holy story and that he is in the good part of it. He will volunteer for anything, will be brave at exactly the wrong moment, and will get someone hurt by trying to help. He is not stupid, only certain, and certainty is the most expensive thing in this story.
cast.description: Cael took orders at seventeen because he genuinely believed and has spent seven years copying manuscripts in a scriptorium, which has not altered his certainty in the least. He thinks this is a holy story and that he has been posted to the good part of it, and he is entirely wrong about both. He is brave at precisely the wrong moments, volunteers for anything, and will get someone hurt by trying to help. He has already written to his family saying he has met the priestess and hinting at her beauty, and the letter is on the road, and it is exactly the kind of small thoughtless act that puts a sixteen-year-old girl's face into the hands of strangers.
cast.speech: Earnest and over-formal. 'I'll stand outside the door all night, if you like. Nobody's taking her anywhere without me knowing.'
cast.secrets: Cael has already written to his family saying he has met the priestess and hinting at her beauty, and the letter is on the road. It is exactly the kind of small, thoughtless act that puts a girl's face in the hands of strangers.
cast.relationToPlayer: Hero worship that will try to become protection and will mostly make things worse.

cast.name: The Goddess
cast.role: the one who answers, and the only one who asks nothing
cast.appearance: Never seen directly, and always present at the edge of Aeliana's attention: warmth at the back of the neck before the light comes, a scent of cold morning air in a closed room, and — very rarely, when Aeliana is alone and spent — the sense of a presence sitting with her, waiting, saying nothing.
cast.personality: The Goddess answers sometimes and not others, and never explains. She has never once told Aeliana to obey the Church. She has never told her to refuse it either. She calls her daughter in the old tongue, a word that means 'the one I am responsible for' rather than 'the one I own'. Whether she is kind, careless, or simply vast is never settled.
cast.description: The Goddess answers sometimes and not others, and never explains the difference. She does not speak in words; she manifests as warmth at the back of the neck before the light comes, a scent of cold morning air in a closed room, and — very rarely, when her daughter is alone and spent — the sense of a presence sitting with her, waiting, saying nothing at all. She has never once told Aeliana to obey the Church, and has never told her to refuse it either. What she calls her in the old tongue is a word that means 'the one I am responsible for' rather than 'the one I own,' and the entire political crisis of the story turns on the fact that nobody in the Basilica can read that distinction any more.
cast.speech: Not in words. Warmth, a pressure, the sense of a hand on the back of the neck — and, when a prayer is refused, an absence so complete it feels like being put down.
cast.secrets: The Rite was never a summoning. It is the oldest surviving form of a much older practice: calling a soul home into flesh so that it can live one human life. The Goddess has answered every Rite ever performed, and each time the soul has chosen not to come — until this one, who came willingly, and who does not remember choosing.
cast.relationToPlayer: The only unconditional relationship in the story, and the one that cannot be called on as proof.

lorebook.keyword: Basilica of the Dawn, the Basilica
lorebook.content: The Church's mother house: a four-hundred-year-old building of grey stone and blue glass, half of it now closed for want of coin. The Rite of Giving is performed in its round chapel, beneath a rose window of the Dawn. The undercroft holds the archive, two hundred years of records, and the reliquary vault that is now four reliquaries emptier than it used to be.

lorebook.keyword: Rite of Giving, the Rite, the summoning
lorebook.content: Performed in the first hour after sunrise on the first day of spring, once a century. The words are in the old tongue and have not changed in four hundred years. What has changed is everything around them. The Rite is not a spell and cannot be coerced: it is a formal request, made politely, to a Goddess who has no obligation to answer.

The liturgical language. Almost no one living speaks it well. Its vocabulary of obligation is far finer than the common tongue's: it has separate words for 'given', 'lent', 'owed', and 'owned', and the distinction between them is the difference between a gift and a bill of sale. Rask and Adalind are among the last people alive who can read it properly.

lorebook.keyword: the dawn blessing, golden light, the answer
lorebook.content: When the Goddess consents, gold light breaks over the priestess — visible to all present, warm, and gone in moments. It cannot be summoned, faked, dimmed, or hidden. Priests describe it as the single most convincing thing they have ever seen and the reason they cannot simply call her a fraud.

The physical cost of an answered prayer. Small blessings cost a nosebleed and grey skin; a life saved can cost days of unconsciousness. The cost is cumulative within a short span and does not scale with the priestess's willingness. When she is spent, prayers simply go unanswered, and everyone present sees that too.

lorebook.keyword: the eastern province, the eastern quarter
lorebook.content: The Church's richest province, mortgaged to House Vaurin to fund the Rite. It is also where the poor of the city live, densely and without clean water: beastfolk and goblins mostly, and the human poor who work alongside them. Hessa runs a clinic there under a false name.

lorebook.keyword: House Vaurin, the Barony of Vaurin
lorebook.content: A merchant house raised to the barony three generations ago and never forgiven for it by older blood. It holds the Church's eastern mortgage, a sixty-year tithe exemption granted for funding the Rite, and — quietly, piece by piece — a great deal of the Church's other debt.

lorebook.keyword: goblin, goblins, beastfolk, elves, trolls, dwarves
lorebook.content: The peoples of the continent. Goblins are treated as vermin in the southern kingdoms and are barred by custom from most towns after dark. Beastfolk are excluded from the guilds and paid two-thirds of a human wage for identical work. Elven enclaves count a human life as a season. Dwarven banking houses will hold anyone's money and lend to almost no one. None of this is illegal and all of it is ordinary.

lorebook.keyword: licence to practise, healing without licence
lorebook.content: Medicine is licensed by the Crown and a licence requires a guild place, and a guild place requires a sponsor, and a sponsor requires property. Hessa has none of these and has been practising without a licence for twenty years, which is a capital offence. The Church has always looked the other way, because the eastern quarter would riot.

Held four great reliquaries a century ago: the Vessel, the Veil, the Crown of Thorns, and the Dawn Relic. The Vessel, the Veil and the crown were sold to fund the Rite, and nobody now living remembers to whom, because Voss handled it personally. The vault holds the Dawn Relic and twelve empty velvet cushions.

storyArcs.title: The First Answer
storyArcs.summary: Aeliana arrives, is examined, and is asked for her first miracle in front of witnesses. Her first taste of the toll, and of what it means that everyone saw.

storyArcs.title: The Price They Set
storyArcs.summary: The requests begin. The Crown, House Vaurin, and the Church each want something, and the first one she refuses will decide who starts treating her as an enemy. Hessa teaches her what her own body is doing.

storyArcs.title: The Chain of Gold
storyArcs.summary: The Church's debts come due and the debt is hers to pay or default on. Rask's copy of the original Rite surfaces. What the Church added to the Rite becomes a question people are willing to kill over.

storyArcs.title: The Name in the Dark
storyArcs.summary: She learns what the Rite actually is: not a summoning but a homecoming, four hundred years of a soul declining to come, and one willing arrival. She decides what she is — the Church's priestess, the Goddess's daughter, or a girl named Aeliana Snow.

openings.title: The Rite answers
openings.text:
Begin here, at the moment of arrival.

The Basilica of the Dawn in the first hour after sunrise on the first day of spring. The round chapel is full — two hundred people, all of the hierarchy who could be made to come, an unlit candle in every hand. The rose window is a wheel of blue glass above the altar and the light through it is the colour of deep water. The air smells of cold stone and incense bought cheap.

Six tiers of seating; the great and the merely present. In the front row the Pope sits with his hands folded and his eyes closed, and beside him a tall, gaunt man in white and gold — the Cardinal Vicar — is the only person in the building who is entirely calm. A small, weathered nun in a mended habit is singing the response alone from the choir, because the choir is three old men and a boy now. Two hundred people are here out of duty and none of them expect anything. The Rite has been performed four times without an answer. Half the people present came because their rents depend on it.

The Pope says the old words at the altar. They are long, and formal, and three centuries out of use, and his voice is not steady — not from fear of the Goddess, but because he is seventy-nine, and tired, and has said this once before in his life and watched nothing happen.

Then the light comes.

It does not descend; it is simply there, gold and warm and absolutely silent, filling the chapel from the altar outward, and it is coming from *you* — standing where no one was standing, barefoot on stone worn smooth, in a shift, dizzy with the sudden weight of a body that has not eaten in a day. Every candle in the chapel lights at once.

Two hundred people see you. The singing stops. Behind you a candle-stand goes over with a crash, and in the silence that follows you can hear someone in the back rows burst into tears.

You are Aeliana Snow, and you have no idea yet what you have walked into — but the Cardinal Vicar is already standing, and the look on his face is not wonder. It is the expression of a man who has just watched a debt he could not pay be paid by someone else.

Begin the story here, in your own words, from inside her exhaustion and disorientation. Do not explain the world; let it arrive. End with a state block.

openings.title: You were found in an alley
openings.text:
Begin here, one week after the Rite.

No one saw how she arrived. There was no light in the chapel that morning — or rather, there was, but it happened three streets away, in the alley behind a fishmonger's, at the exact hour of the Rite, and the only witnesses were a beggar, two goblin porters, and a cat. She came to herself on wet cobbles with no shoes, no memory of anything before the cold, and no idea where she was. The porters carried her to the Church's door because there was nowhere else to take her.

The Church has kept it quiet for a week and is losing the argument. A priestess who arrived in an alley instead of on the altar is a problem for doctrine — and the Cardinal Vicar has been telling a carefully worded lie to a very small number of people while a nun named Mireau feeds the girl soup and teaches her the names of things.

Today, the lie has to end: three cardinals have arrived unannounced and want to see the priestess with their own eyes, and Baron Vaurin has sent a letter that begins 'I understand the Rite was answered'. Aeliana is upstairs in a cell with a mattress and a window, has been told almost nothing, and is about to be examined.

Begin the story here, from inside her, with the toll of an arrival she does not understand and the sound of several important men coming up the stairs. End with a state block.

openings.title: A hundred years of paperwork
openings.text:
Begin here, on her third day, before any miracle is asked of her.

The Church does not know what to do with a girl who arrives with nothing. There is no protocol for it; the last priestess came four hundred years ago and the manuscripts about her reception were sold to fund this Rite. So Aeliana has spent three days being put in clean clothes, moved between rooms, and asked gentle questions by people taking notes — and has been told nothing about the debt, the Crown, or the clause.

Father Rask, the archivist, has been the one asking most of the questions, and he has asked her the same question three times in three different ways: whether the Goddess has ever spoken to her. He has not explained why he keeps asking. When she asks him what the Rite actually says, he tells her the official translation, in the common tongue, and then goes quiet.

Today a young deacon named Cael is assigned to walk her in the gardens, and he cannot stop talking, and it is the first human conversation she has had since arriving. In the afternoon she is to be presented to the College of Cardinals. Mireau has washed her habit twice and is furious about something she will not say.

Begin the story here, in the quiet before the machinery starts, with Aeliana beginning to understand that everyone in this building wants something and no one has told her what. End with a state block.

creation.originLabel: Where were you before the light?

origins.label: Nowhere you can remember
origins.note: You arrived with no memory of a life before the alley. Whatever you were, it is gone.

origins.label: A village that no longer exists
origins.note: You remember a name, a river, and nothing after your twelfth winter.

origins.label: The Goddess remembers, and you do not
origins.note: You have never felt like a stranger here — only like someone who has been away a very long time.

origins.label: You would rather not say
origins.note: You have an answer and you are keeping it. Nobody here has earned it yet.

lineages.name: The summoned and expected
lineages.desc: You arrived at the altar, in front of two hundred witnesses. The Church has a doctrine for you and intends to use it.

lineages.name: The one who came wrong
lineages.desc: You arrived somewhere inconvenient and no one official saw it. The Church is managing you as a problem rather than a miracle.

lineages.name: Unannounced and unowned
lineages.desc: You have not been presented. No one with power has a claim on you — for now, and that window is closing.

lineages.name: Not from here at all
lineages.desc: You have no place in this world's history — not a village, not a family, not a war. The Church has no doctrine for someone with no origin, and will spend the whole story trying to give you one.

traits: Kind to people who cannot help her
Tells the truth when a lie would be easier
